title: STOMATIN-DEFICIENT CRYOHYDROCYTOSIS WITH NEUROLOGIC DEFECTS

intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that stomatin-deficient cryohydrocytosis with neurologic defects (SDCHCN) is caused by mutation in the SLC2A1 gene, which encodes the glucose transporter GLUT1.

checks.explanation: The title also says sdCHC 'results from mutations in SLC2A1'.

checks.explanation: The abstract states that SLC2A1 encodes GLUT1.

paragraphs.text: Stomatin-deficient cryohydrocytosis with neurologic defects is a rare form of hereditary stomatocytosis. Red cells leak monovalent cations, and the leak increases on cooling. Patients have hemolytic anemia and hepatosplenomegaly, together with cataracts, seizures, mental retardation, and movement disorder (Fricke et al., 2004; Flatt et al., 2011). The disorder is a form of GLUT1 deficiency syndrome in which SLC2A1 mutations cause both loss of glucose transport and a red cell cation leak (Flatt et al., 2011). Temperature-dependent loss of potassium from red cells can cause pseudohyperkalemia (Bawazir et al., 2012).

paragraphs.text: Fricke et al. (2004) studied red cells from 3 new isolated cases and 1 new pedigree of stomatin-deficient hereditary stomatocytosis, and expanded on 1 previously reported case. The cases differed in how the passive potassium leak depended on temperature. In 2 cases the leak was lowest at around 20 to 25 degrees C, so the cells were extremely leaky at 0 degrees C, giving the cryohydrocytosis phenotype. Fricke et al. (2004) said these were the only 2 known cases of stomatin-deficient cryohydrocytosis. Both patients had a congenital syndrome of mental retardation, seizures, cataracts, and massive hepatosplenomegaly, which the authors suggested probably defined a new hemato-neurologic syndrome.

paragraphs.text: Bawazir et al. (2012) reported an infant who presented with erratic hyperkalemia, neonatal hyperbilirubinemia, anemia, hepatic dysfunction, and microcephaly. Seizures and delayed developmental milestones followed. Brain MRI and CT scans showed multiple abnormalities, including periventricular calcification. The infant had visual impairment caused by both cataracts and retinal dysfunction. The red cells were extremely leaky, which caused the hemolysis. Potassium loss from the red cells depended on temperature, which explained the hyperkalemia as pseudohyperkalemia. Bawazir et al. (2012) stated that this was the fourth pedigree described with this syndrome.

paragraphs.text: Lande et al. (1982) studied the erythrocyte membrane proteins of 2 patients with congenital hemolytic anemia caused by increased red cell permeability to sodium and potassium; 1 patient had hereditary stomatocytosis and the other had cryohydrocytosis. SDS gel electrophoresis separated band 7 into components of about 30,000, 28,000, and 26,000 daltons. The 28,000-dalton component was decreased in both patients. Two-dimensional electrophoresis split this component into 2 proteins, designated 22 x 8 and 60 x 8. Protein 22 x 8 was completely absent in both patients, whereas 60 x 8 was present. All band 7 proteins were present in normal subjects and in reticulocytosis controls.

paragraphs.text: In all of their cases, Fricke et al. (2004) found by Western blotting that red cell membranes were deficient in the 32-kD membrane protein stomatin. All showed marked cation leaks at 37 degrees C and markedly abnormal intracellular sodium and potassium concentrations. Immunocytochemistry showed that the stomatin deficiency was not complete. On typical blood films, some red cells were stomatin-positive while most were negative, although in 1 case only a minority were negative. All platelets and neutrophils were stomatin-positive.
